parts.role: monitor (x2), cost-down twin of the primary if the dock drives both screens
parts.product: Samsung ViewFinity S6 S60D 27" QHD (no USB-C)
parts.price_source: samsung.com/us list $329.99 (2026-11-07). Amazon regional deal $160.37 (Slickdeals 2025-07-28). Typical street estimate $180-230.
pros: Same 612.9x367.7x41.6 mm, 3.6 kg chassis as the S60UD, so the same CAD works
About $100-150 cheaper per unit
cons: No USB-C and no DP-out. Only works if the cradle dock provides two separate video outputs (which macOS needs anyway).
parts.notes: Same housing per Samsung's spec, so assume the same rear box and VESA geometry, but check port positions (no USB-C, DP-out or RJ45). Decide this together with the dock architecture.

design_implications: The monitors stay whole in their own housings: mains stays inside the certified monitor. The SPEC's 'stripped LCD module' (module_t 10 mm) and 'display_boards' parts must go. Model each facet as a full housing: for the S60UD, a 612.9 x 362.6 mm face plus the 40 x 5.2 mm centre logo nub, a 16 mm edge band and a 449 x 211 x 39.6 mm rear box centred on the face.

Seam: the two inner bezels give 16.16 mm (S60UD); 16.56 (PA278CFRV); 15.76 (P2725DE). With about 0.5-1.0 mm assembly gap, set seam_mm to about 17 (params currently 14). The metal-look strip (4 mm) sits on the joint and does not hide bezel. inner_border/outer_border 7/9 become 8.08/8.08. top_border 9 becomes about 6.8. chin 16 becomes about 20.0, plus the nub. Active 596.7 x 335.7 is unchanged.

Toe-in 10 deg about a vertical axis at the front inner corners (the seam axis): outer edges at x=±603.6, z=+106.4 mm. The pair chord is 1207 mm over housings (about 1213 with a 3 mm frame lip), which matches the SPEC's ~1214. With the S60UD (VESA face 39.6 mm behind the screen), the VESA centres are at x=±308.7, z=+14.2 relative to the seam point on the screen plane, 617 mm apart, with mounting faces rotated ±10 deg. Use a steel spine with two ±10 deg VESA plates, or an adjustable dual arm. The printed shroud must not carry the 7.2 kg of monitors.

The backs diverge behind the seam: the rim inner rear corners sit at x=±2.8, z=-15.8. The S60UD rear-box inner corners sit at x=±87.6, z=-24.8, leaving a central channel about 175 mm wide behind the seam for the 36 x 38 mm post, VESA hub and cables.

VESA height: on the S60UD the VESA centre is at the centre of the housing face (181.2 mm above the face bottom edge, centred left-right). If the glass bottom stays at y=156, the VESA centres sit at y≈337 (params vesa_hub y=262 must move up or be recomputed). The active-area centre is about 6.8 mm above the VESA centre.

Rear shroud depth: the S60UD needs at least 41.6 + 2 (steel plate) + 6-10 (air gap) = about 50-54 mm behind the screen at the rear box, but only about 16-20 mm over the 16 mm edge band (this matches the SPEC's 16 mm 'shroud_thin' zone). The current 45 mm shroud_depth is too shallow. PA278CFRV needs about 52-55 mm; Dell about 58 mm.

Heat: both picks have internal PSUs (S60UD 160 W max rated, about 20-25 W typical; extra loss when it supplies 90 W PD). Do not seal the rear box. Keep at least 10 mm air gap over the box and put intake slots on the shroud underside and exhaust slots along the top (chimney flow). No printed part should touch the box vents. Prefer PETG/ASA over PLA near the box.

Cables (S60UD): video, USB-C and DP-out face down from the rear-box underside at x=+72.6...+212.4 mm (front-view right of centre), 76 mm above the face bottom. Plugs drop into the space behind the bottom rim (13-34 mm behind the screen). Use up-angle/right-angle DP, HDMI and USB-C plugs and leave the shroud bottom open there. The AC inlet faces down at x=-137.5...-168.5 (likely IEC C14, 31 x 21.5 mm body); use a right-angle C13 cord. Side-facing USB-A, RJ45 and headphone ports on the +x face of the rear box (x=+224.5, 179-268 mm above face bottom): on the left monitor they open into the central channel, on the right monitor toward the right wing. Leave 50 mm clearance or plan not to use them.

Controls: the S60UD's only control is a rear joystick at bottom centre (x=0, 39-62 mm above the face bottom, 7 mm proud of the rim back). The shroud needs a finger opening of about 35 x 35 mm, or a printed plunger. Keep the front power-LED nub clear (or let the front frame notch around it). For the PA278CFRV, the OSD keys are on the chin's front-right (x≈+187...+283), so the front frame bottom rail must leave them exposed. The hard power switch is in the rear bay.

Front frame: the S60UD chin has a lip about 2 mm proud of the screen plane over its bottom ~18 mm (from the 3D model). The bottom rail of the printed frame must step over it. Lip coverage on the outer bezel is at most about 5 mm, or it shades active pixels at the 10 deg toe-in.

Docking link: put the USB-C-host monitor on the RIGHT (nearest the right-wing cradle). Cradle plug, then a full-featured, e-marked 5 A USB-C cable (≤1 m passive) to the right monitor's USB-C (90 W PD + DP alt), then DP-out (MST) to the left monitor's DP-in. On the S60UD the right monitor's USB-C sits about 380-520 mm from the seam along the facet, i.e. toward the cradle.

Bandwidth: two QHD@100 Hz streams over one USB-C need 4-lane DP (about 18.8 of 25.9 Gbps HBR3). If the monitor runs 2-lane DP + USB 3 hub (12.96 Gbps), both screens drop to 60 Hz. Expect to set the USB-C mode to 'high resolution / USB 2.0' in the OSD, at the cost of a slow hub, or accept 60 Hz.

Mac: macOS does not support MST extended desktops (the second screen mirrors), and base M1/M2 MacBooks drive only one external display (M3 base: two only with the lid closed, which suits this cradle). For the 'universal' cradle, the dock must output two independent DP streams (TB3/TB4/USB4 dock with 2 outputs, or DisplayLink for M1/M2). If the dock does this, the monitors' USB-C is optional and the cheaper S60D twin (same chassis) works.

Power strip: 2 outlets for the monitors (one IEC cord each, 100-240 V internal PSUs). Budget up to 160 W each worst case. The monitors can also charge the laptop at 90 W, so no separate laptop charger is needed on the Windows/one-cable path.
risks: Price: the S60UD lists at $369.99, above the $330 cap. It needs a sale (about $300 seen; Black Friday 2026-11-27). The PA278CFRV swings $190-$330 and its stock is patchy (2023 model). The Dell P2725DE is about $425. The pair costs about $500-600 of the $1,200 budget.

S60UD top/bottom bezels, chin lip, VESA centre and port positions come from Samsung's 3D model and official photos, not a mechanical drawing (expect ±1 mm, ±2-3 mm for VESA). The side bezel (8.08) is computed from official W minus active W, assuming a centred active area (the photos agree). Measure the first unit with calipers before printing the front frame and seam parts.

The VESA centre on the S60UD was taken from the stand's VESA plate in the 3D model. The Easy Setup Stand hooks in, so the VESA holes could be recessed or covered. Have M4x10/12/16/20 screws and 5-10 mm spacers ready.

Panel matching: buy both units together from one retailer (same panel revision and firmware) to limit tint and uniformity mismatch, which an 'honest seam' design makes obvious. IPS glow differs between units.
Enclosing internal-PSU monitors in a shroud can raise temperatures. Thermal-test with 90 W PD charging and full brightness, and keep vents open.

USB-C cable length and quality from a sprung cradle plug (the 90 W PD + DP-alt link) is the weakest link. Passive full-featured cables are limited to about 1 m, and extension or pogo stages can drop DP alt mode.
macOS cannot extend over MST. A Mac-universal cradle needs a dual-output dock, or the left screen mirrors.
open_questions: Dock architecture decides the monitor choice. Will the cradle feed one monitor's USB-C (MST daisy chain, Windows-first), or a TB/USB4/DisplayLink dock with two outputs (Mac-safe)? With a dual-output dock, the S60D (no USB-C, about $100-150 cheaper each, same chassis) is enough.

Is 2x100 Hz over the single cradle cable required? If so, the monitor's USB-C must run 4-lane DP (USB 2.0 hub), so confirm the S60UD exposes this OSD setting (the manual only describes the MST/SST DP-out mode and a 'Max. Power Saving' option).
Budget split: is about $600 for the pair acceptable, or should the build default to the PA278CFRV (about $400-500 for the pair, deeper 44.9 mm wedge back, 4.9 kg)?
Confirm on arrival (S60UD): AC inlet type (C14 assumed), VESA hole depth relative to the box back, exact top and bottom bezels, side-port positions, and the joystick location. Then finalise params.
Is the 2 mm proud chin lip and 5 mm logo nub acceptable for the front-frame design, or should the frame's bottom rail be cut out around the nub?

The S60UD keeps its USB 3.0 hub and LAN live over USB-C, which points to fixed 2-lane DP. The manual timing table gives 2560x1440@100 RB = 410.5 MHz, which is 9.85 Gbps per stream at 8 bpc and 19.7 Gbps for two. Two-lane HBR3 carries 12.96 Gbps, so expect both screens at 60 Hz over USB-C MST. Only DP-in MST is documented at 2x QHD@100 (manual p23). HDR is disabled in MST. The official front render gives about 6.6 and 19.5. The report says 6.8 and 20.0. Side bezels check out at 8.2-8.4 each. (5) Ventilation: manual p11 requires 10 cm clearance at the top, sides and back, so a close-fitting rear shroud goes against Samsung's install guidance. verify.summary:
I checked both picks against Samsung's and ASUS's own spec pages and manuals, and parsed Samsung's 3D model myself. Both are real products with correct MPNs, but each needs corrections.

Samsung S60UD (LS27D606UANXGO, primary): still sold, at $369.99 on samsung.com/us today, and its official dimensions, weight, VESA, power and ports all check out. Plan on $330-370 each; $300 only on a sale.
1. The VESA depth is wrong. The VESA holes sit in a 120.2 x 120.2 mm pocket 8.2 mm deep, about 31.4 mm behind the screen face, not 39.6. At 10 deg toe-in the VESA centre moves to x=±307.3, z=+22.3 (they had 308.7 / 14.2). A VESA plate wider than 120 mm needs 8.5-9 mm spacers, which puts it back at about 40 mm.
2. The single-cable 100 Hz plan doesn't work as written. The setting they planned to use to free up DisplayPort bandwidth on the USB-C port exists only on the S80UD. Two 1440p streams at 100 Hz need about 19.7 Gbps, more than the roughly 13 Gbps the port likely carries, so expect both screens at 60 Hz when daisy-chained from USB-C. Samsung documents 2 x 100 Hz only from the DisplayPort input.
3. The top and bottom bezels are only known to about ±2 mm. The model's screen texture gives a top bezel of about 8.5 mm and a chin of about 18.8 mm. Samsung's front render gives about 6.6 and 19.5 mm. Design the frame so it never covers more than 6.5 mm at the top or 18.5 mm at the bottom.
4. Samsung's manual asks for 10 cm of free space at the top, sides and back, which a close rear shroud conflicts with.
5. The power inlet is very likely IEC C14, so use a right-angle C13 cord.

ASUS PA278CFRV (alternate): its specs and outline drawing check out within about 1 mm. The '7.9' in the drawing is the top-edge depth, though the top bezel does measure about 7.8 mm.
- The VESA screws are specified after all: M4 x 10 mm, with a mount rated for at least 5.85 kg.
- It is better than the Samsung for one-cable daisy chaining: ASUS documents daisy chain over USB-C at 1440p 100 Hz and has a setting to give the display the full link.
- The real risk is stock: I found no US listing in stock today. The last deals were $199 in April 2026 and $249 in January 2026; list is $329.

Two corrections to their design notes:
- Of the base-chip Macs, only the M3 MacBook Air drives two external screens, and only with the lid closed. The base M3 MacBook Pro drives one. Base M4 models drive two with the lid open.
- Use the manual's 410.5 MHz pixel clock for bandwidth: about 9.85 Gbps per 1440p 100 Hz stream.

design_implications: RECOMMENDED APPROACH = native-first hybrid Thunderbolt 4 dock with built-in DisplayLink fallback (TBT-6950PD). Per laptop family: M3 Air/Pro (dual only lid-closed, macOS 14.6+, and the cradle is always lid-closed), M4/M5/M6 and every Pro/Max, Intel TB3 Macs, Windows/Linux with TB3/TB4/TB5/USB4 -> 2 native screens, no driver. Base M1/M2 (hardware limit: 1 external display; no dock raises it) -> 1 native + 1 DisplayLink. Windows/Linux with plain USB-C DP-alt -> DisplayLink (or 2 native via MST only with an MST dock like TBT4-UDZ). MacBook Neo (A18 Pro, USB 3 + DP1.4 alt on the left port only, 1 external display, no Thunderbolt) -> only USB-C DisplayLink docks are verified (alternate UD-6950PDH). Pure MST docks and monitor daisy-chaining fail on every Mac because macOS has no MST extend.

Monitor wiring for the primary (inside the shroud): monitor L DP-in <- TB4 DFP #1 via USB-C(male, DP alt)->DP cable; monitor R DP-in <- TB4 DFP #2 via a second USB-C->DP cable; if the owner's laptop is base M1/M2, also run monitor R HDMI-in <- DisplayLink HDMI #1 and enable monitor auto-input. Install DisplayLink Manager only on laptops that need it (otherwise macOS creates a third, duplicate display). Budget 2x USB-C->DP + 1x HDMI cable, 1.5-2 m (route up the neck).

Dock location: NOT in the cradle (cavity under the slot floor is only 18.5 mm, y 2.5..21, and the plug carriage occupies it). Put it in the base's right end, long axis along x, host-port side face toward +x/cradle. Base interior is 25 mm (params: deck_y 30 - deck_t 2.5, floor_t 2.5): TBT-6950PD 17 mm fits with 8 mm air; SD5900T 22 mm marginal; TBT-UDM 23 mm marginal; UD-6950PDH 24.5 mm needs base height ~40 mm (cavity >= 28); TBT4-UDZ 35 mm does not fit.

Dock bay clearances: >= 70 mm plan clearance behind the rear (210 x 17) face for HDMI/USB-C->DP overmolds plus horizontal bends (no room to bend vertically in 25 mm); >= 45 mm beside the host side face for the cable's straight end (Newnex straight overmold 35 mm incl. strain relief, 12.2 x 6.4); optional front cut-out ~ 60 x 14 mm to expose the dock's 2x USB-A 10G = user USB ports. Stand the dock on 2-3 mm ribs, add inlet/outlet vents (dock ambient spec for this class 0-40 C), print the bay in PETG/ASA, not PLA.

Safety: the dock's brick (180 W, 21 V, IEC C5/C6 cord) stays outside the base, plugged into the certified power strip; only DC enters the base. The current CAD still has base.ac_inlet (x=400) and internals.psu (x 330..470) from the computer-in-base concept: delete both (they imply user mains wiring).

Cradle plug = one end of the dock's own male-male host cable. Never a male-female extension (non-compliant per USB Type-C; breaks the 5 A e-marker so charging can drop to 60 W, and 40 Gbps signal integrity). For the TB4 hybrid the cable must be USB4/TB4 40 Gbps + 5 A e-marked; the DisplayLink alternate only needs 5 Gbps but use the same cable.

A right-angle plug is mandatory with the current cradle: straight overmold 35 mm + >= 25 mm bend radius >> 18.5 mm cavity. Use the side-exit (left/right, Newnex 'CR5') head: 15.51 mm along the mating axis, 12.35 (z) x 6.50 (x), cable leaves along -z (toward the hinge end and the base) at ~7.8 mm below the overmold face, OD 4.8 mm. Rotate the plug 180 deg about y to pick +z or -z exit (USB-C is reversible).

Update CAD dock.connector: plug [2.40, 6.65, 8.25] (x thickness, y exposed length, z width) per USB Type-C spec Fig 3-3 (8.25+-0.03 x 2.40+-0.03, 6.65+-0.10); boot/overmold [6.50, 15.51, 12.35] with its face at y = 23.6 (landing plane 24.0 minus delta 0.4), i.e. boot_y [8.09, 23.6]; strain relief continues 34.5 - 6.18 = 28.3 mm from the plug centre along -z. The old boot [7, 6, 14] / boot_y [18, 24] is not a real overmold.

Seating geometry: the laptop must land on the slot floor/pads, never on the plug. Per USB Type-C Fig 3-80 a fully seated plug leaves >= 0.05 mm between the overmold face and the product surface, so set the overmold face delta = 0.3-0.5 mm BELOW the landing plane (adjust with 0.2 mm printed shims); the plug then sits within ~0.5 mm of full depth with zero laptop weight on the port. Put two 1 mm felt/TPU landing pads on the floor away from the plug and define the landing plane at their tops.

Floating carriage: printed block gripping the CR5 head (walls 1.6 mm -> body ~9.7 x 37.7 x 17.1 mm, bottom at y ~6.5), with a flange (>= 20 x 40 mm) under the slot floor that overlaps the floor hole by >= 2 mm at full float. That flange also retains it against the 8-20 N extraction pull when the laptop is lifted. Floor hole ~13.3 (x) x 19.2 (z) mm (boss 9.7 x 15.6 + 2 x 1.5 float + 2 x 0.3), chamfered on top. Housing pocket under the slot ~37 (x) x 57 (z) mm; it fits x 703..741 around the slot axis x=722.

Centring: 4x McMaster 9657K614 at the carriage corners, axes at 45 deg in plan, in Dia 5.0 mm pockets 7.0 mm installed (1.72 N preload each) with Dia 3.2 mm locating pips. That gives float +-1.5 mm per axis, 1.37 N/mm per axis, <= 2.05 N restoring force, and yaw self-centring. No vertical spring: a vertical preload above the 20 N max insertion force would press the carriage onto its seat and the friction would kill the low-force lateral float. Seat the carriage on PTFE-faced surfaces with 0.2-0.3 mm vertical capture clearance.

Tilt relief: let the carriage rock +-2-3 deg (raised contact ridge on the flange right around the plug, >= 1 mm clearance at the carriage ends, crowned seat). Then a laptop lifted one end first, which pivots in its own plane and is not stopped by the slot walls, cannot wrench the port. Lateral float alone absorbs about 0.3 mm per 1.6 deg at a 10 mm lever.

Pre-alignment is the inserts' job: the plug tip has almost no lead-in (8.25 plug in a ~8.34 receptacle), so the slot must deliver the port to within +-0.5 mm. The width insert registers the laptop's bottom face against one wall (relief channels for rubber feet). A depth insert sets z-clearance <= 1 mm and registers the hinge end against the -z end wall. The carriage sled is adjustable along z over at least 15-120 mm from the hinge-end wall (MacBook ports are on the left side near the hinge) and in x via shims, because port height above the laptop's bottom face varies by model.

Slot length: CAD slot z = 224 mm (z -112..112) fits MacBook Air 13 (21.5 cm deep) and MacBook Pro 14 (22.12 cm) but not MacBook Air 15 (23.76 cm), MacBook Pro 16 (24.81 cm) or most 15-16 in PCs. For the 'universal' claim make the slot >= 255 mm or open-ended with depth inserts (Apple specs pages, 2026-11-07).

Cable routing in the cradle: run the cable flat in the cavity (OD 4.8 mm in an 18.5 mm space) with a horizontal service loop of R >= 25 mm (USB Type-C flex test uses 3.7 x OD = 18 mm) and ~100 mm free length. Clamp it with a printed P-clip 60-100 mm from the carriage so cable stiffness does not bias the float, then route it into the base at the x=650 joint. The Newnex 1 m cable leaves ~0.6 m to coil in the base (coil Dia >= 60 mm), or order a custom ~0.4 m length (Newnex minimum 127 mm).

Gravity and lift numbers (USB Type-C R2.0 s3.8.1): insertion 5-20 N, which the spec says 'does not apply when used in a docking application'; extraction 8-20 N new, 6-20 N after 10,000 cycles. Laptop weights: MacBook Air 13 1.23 kg = 12.1 N, Air 15 1.51 kg = 14.8 N, Pro 14 1.55-1.62 kg = 15.2-15.9 N, Pro 16 2.14 kg = 21.0 N, ultralight PCs ~1.0 kg = 9.8 N. So heavier laptops self-seat, and a 1.0-1.25 kg laptop self-seats only if its port needs less force than its weight (otherwise a light press of <= 1 kgf). Lift-out = weight + extraction = ~20-32 N for an Air 13: easy, and nothing to unlock.

Side-load budget: the USB-C 4-axis continuity test loads a right-angle receptacle with 20 N at 15 mm (0.30 Nm). The carriage's worst-case 2 N at ~8 mm is ~0.016 Nm (about 5%). The plug survives 0.75 Nm with no damage and fails at 2.0 Nm (up/down) / 3.5 Nm (left/right), so the slot walls (>= 36 mm tall, ~1 mm total clearance -> tilt <= ~1.6 deg) plus carriage rock keep the port far below those limits.

Seated light without a switch: either (a) a tiny USB microcontroller (e.g. RP2040 board) on a dock USB port that lights the amber 'seated' strip only when the laptop's USB host has enumerated it (the dock's downstream ports stay powered when undocked, so VBUS alone is not a valid signal), or (b) an IR reflective proximity sensor in the slot floor. Don't tap the TB4 cable.

OS behaviour in the cradle (always lid-closed): macOS clamshell works with power + external display; Apple-silicon MacBooks boot when power is connected, so re-seating the laptop powers it on. Wake a sleeping Mac from an external keyboard (Bluetooth wake allowed). Windows: set lid-close to 'Do nothing' on AC; cold-boot with the lid shut needs a BIOS 'power on with AC attach' or similar option, which is model-specific. Linux: logind HandleLidSwitchDocked=ignore; enroll the dock with boltctl; DisplayLink needs the Synaptics evdi driver.
risks: Budget: the hybrid path costs ~$300 dock + $65 cable + ~$10 springs + ~$40 video cables, about $415, or ~35% of the $1,200 total. If the owner's laptop is known, TBT-UDM ($199.95, M3/M4/M5/Pro/TB PCs) or UD-6950PDH ($179.95, base M1/M2/Neo) cuts it to ~$250.

DisplayLink screens (alternate dock; one screen on base M1/M2 with the primary): compression on motion, CPU/GPU load, 60 Hz cap at 1440p, no HDCP (streaming services won't play), driver breakage after OS updates, macOS Screen Recording permission. Not suitable for gaming.

MacBook Neo: Thunderbolt docks (incl. the primary) are not on Plugable's Neo-tested list, and Plugable states TB docks are not compatible. Only USB-C DisplayLink docks (alternate UD-6950PDH, UD-ULTC4K) are verified.

Gravity seating may fail on light (~1.0-1.25 kg) laptops whose ports need close to the spec maximum of 20 N insertion force. That needs a light press, which partially breaks the 'its own weight seats it' story. Bench-test the target laptop with a luggage scale before finalising.

Port wear and side-loading: USB-C is rated for 10,000 cycles (~14 years at 2 docks/day). The real danger is a one-ended lift or a dropped laptop levering the plug. Mitigated by tight inserts, tilt-relief carriage, delta gap so the laptop never bears on the plug, and soft float springs.

Mis-registration: if the insert/sled settings put the port more than ~0.5 mm off the plug tip, the plug stubs on the chassis instead of entering. Users must set the carriage per laptop (needs a printed setup gauge and instructions).

Newnex cable: product page says 80 Gbps Gen4x2 but the drawing title says 40 Gbps, and it is not Intel TB4-certified (USB4-compliant only). The Plugable/Cable Matters alternates are certified but publish no head dimensions, and their angle direction must be checked on arrival.
Mixed households: on a base M1/M2 the single native stream may go to either TB4 DFP. The 'R monitor has native DP + DisplayLink HDMI' wiring trick needs testing; the fallback is re-wiring per laptop.
Kensington SD5900T (candidate) is officially macOS-only on the US SKU. TBT4-UDZ lists Linux as not supported. Linux support in general is 'works in practice' only.
Thermal: a TB4 + DisplayLink dock passing 96 W sits in a closed 25 mm printed cavity. Without vents it can exceed its 40 C ambient rating and soften PLA.
Dock brick dimensions (180 W) are unpublished, so plan an under-desk/power-strip location rather than a fixed pocket.
CAD drift: the current params have a fictional connector overmold (boot [7,6,14]), a 224 mm slot, base.ac_inlet and internals.psu. All conflict with real parts or the no-mains rule.
open_questions: Which laptop(s) will actually be docked (M3/M4/M5 Air only, any base M1/M2, MacBook Neo, which Windows/Linux models)? That decides hybrid vs TBT-UDM vs UD-6950PDH and whether the DisplayLink HDMI run is needed.

Do the chosen 27 in QHD monitors have DP + HDMI (needed for the dual-input fallback) or USB-C/DP-alt inputs (could take TB4 DFP directly)? Is >60 Hz wanted? Native TB4 DFP DP 1.4 should carry 1440p at 100-165 Hz but Plugable only documents 60 Hz; DisplayLink is 60 Hz.
Final base height: stay at 36 mm (25 mm cavity -> only the 17 mm TBT-6950PD fits comfortably) or go to ~40-44 mm so any slim dock fits? Or mount the dock under the desk?

Can Newnex supply U4T1C01CR5P010 in a ~0.4 m custom length (minimum 127 mm), and at what MOQ/price? Otherwise coil ~0.6 m in the base.

Should the slot be lengthened (>= 255 mm or open-ended) so MacBook Air 15 / Pro 16 and 15-16 in PCs fit, as 'universal' implies?

I checked all six primary and alternate parts against Plugable, Newnex and NTC pages, the Newnex drawings and the USB Type-C R2.0 spec. None is rejected. Two are corrected, two are verified as stated and the two McMaster springs could not be checked. Notes are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-NatesApps/d849125a-a5da-5c83-991f-43ec8426b1a4/scratchpad/research/dock-verify/notes.md.

**Primary dock, Plugable TBT-6950PD: corrected (minor).** Price, size and specs are confirmed:
- $299.99 at plugable.com; $299.95 at Walmart and Zones.
- 17 x 210 x 95 mm, 470 g.
- Host port is a TB4 port on the right-hand side face (seen from the front), giving 96 W.
- 180 W brick, 21 V / 8.58 A, IEC C5/C6.
- 3x TB4 downstream ports (DP 1.4) plus 2x DisplayLink HDMI.

Plugable's FAQ confirms the display counts the report gives per Mac. Three corrections:
- **Plain USB-C laptops (no Thunderbolt/USB4):** Plugable says these are "not supported". The report's "DisplayLink outputs" for them is not a documented mode.
- **Power button:** the dock has a front power button and LED. It turns on by itself when plugged in, but a press turns it off until pressed again, so the base cut-out should reach it.
- **Heat:** the aluminium case is the heatsink, which supports the report's advice to vent the cavity.

**Alternate dock, Plugable UD-6950PDH: verified.** 24.5 x 225 x 85 mm, 465 g. USB-C 5 Gbps host port on the rear, 100 W, 130 W brick. Plugable lists it as passing on the MacBook Neo. $199.99 list; $179.95 at Best Buy. On a Neo it must plug into the left (USB 3) port.

**Primary cable, Newnex U4T1C01CR5P010: corrected.** It is $64.99 and in stock at NTC. Side-exit and the main dimensions are confirmed: plug 8.25 x 2.40 x 6.65 mm, head 15.51 / 6.50 / 34.50 mm, and a 12.35 mm full-depth zone centred on the plug. I measured the drawing PDF at 600 dpi and found three CAD errors:
- **Cable axis:** it sits 9.19 mm from the overmold face (6.34 mm below the head's back face), not 7.8 mm. In the cradle CAD that puts the axis at y = 14.41.
- **Strain relief:** it is about 8.4 x 8.4 mm in section, larger than the 6.5 mm head, so the planned 9.7 mm-wide carriage can't hold it. The pocket needs about 8.6 mm inside there.
- **Rest of the head:** past the full-depth zone the head steps back 2.84 mm from the overmold face. At boot_y [8.09, 23.6] that surface sits at y = 20.76, only 0.24 mm under the slot floor's underside. The planned 2-3 degree carriage rock would jam it, so the underside of the floor needs a relief of at least 1.5 mm, or the rock must be limited.

All the report's USB Type-C spec figures match the spec: plug tolerances, insertion/extraction forces and their docking exemptions, side-load and wrenching limits, 0.05 mm overmold clearance, and the flex test.

The numbers the report quotes are self-consistent with spring physics, and its preload and force maths are right. One design problem it missed: with spring axes at 45 degrees, a ±1.5 mm float pushes each spring end up to 2.1 mm sideways, so the Ø3.2 locating pips will make them bow or pop off. Use a flat seat on the carriage or limit float to about ±1 mm.

design_implications: BASE HEIGHT / POWER BAY: at 36 mm the base cavity is only about 25 mm clear (floor 2.5 to deck 27.5), and no certified mains product fits. Make the base 50 mm tall at least along the rear power spine (z about -146 to -60) and at the right-end brick bay, giving 43 mm or more of clear height. If the base must stay 36 mm, move all power gear into a separate printed under-desk tray and keep only 12 V and 5 V in the base.

POWER STRIP POCKET (Tripp Lite PS2406RA08B): reserve 615 x 45 x 36 mm (envelope 609.6 x 40.9 x 31.8 mm, measure on arrival) along the rear inside wall. Lay it on edge with the outlet face vertical so plugs go in horizontally; keep a 30 mm right-angle-plug zone in front of the outlet face and 51 mm cord-bend space at the cord end. Outlets are at 144 mm centres. Fix it only with its own clips screwed to printed bosses (M3 heat-set inserts); never drill or open it.

MAINS CORD EXIT: one printed strain-relief clamp or grommet at the rear for the strip's 14/3 SJT cord (allow a 10.5 mm cord OD and pass the right-angle plug through a removable hatch, or route the cord before closing). This is the only mains cord leaving the base. Leave a rear window over the strip's lighted switch (with its clear cover) so it works as the master switch.

Every load cord into the strip must have a right-angle or low-profile NEMA plug (P007-002-15D to C13 for monitors with C14 inlets; a right-angle 1-15P to C7 cord for the Monoprice charger and for the dock brick if it uses C7). No wall-wart chargers can live in the base: only desktop bricks with IEC cords.

GaN CHARGER POCKET (Monoprice 46820): 98.81 W x 76.31 D x 23.10 H mm (body 22.10, feet 1 mm; foot centres 17.1 mm from the sides and 25.1 mm from the long faces). USB-C1, C2, C3 and USB-A are on one long face, 1.2 mm inset; the IEC C8 inlet is on the opposite long face. Keep 35 mm clear in front of the ports (right-angle USB-C cables recommended) and 30 mm behind the inlet. Put it near the LV hub (left end, the old compute zone x -600..-300 is free) and over an intake vent.

LV HUB: a WAGO 221 carrier plate (about 100 x 60 mm) next to the charger holds Adafruit 5807 (24.5 x 20.2 x 4.9), Pololu D36V6F5 (13 x 10 x 3), 3x TLP627M on a perfboard scrap (about 30 x 20 mm), Adafruit 6032 (reserve 40 x 20 x 15), the LDP-2A dimmer (61 x 33 x 32) and Adafruit 368 (reserve 35 x 15 x 15). Wiring: C1 to Adafruit 6032 (12 V) to the LDP-2A dimmer to Adafruit 368 to a dimmed 12 V Wago pair, which feeds the under-glow halves, the neck bar and the three indicator segments (each indicator in series with its TLP627M C-E). C2 to Adafruit 5807 (12 V) to an aux 12 V Wago pair, which feeds the Qi boards (if they take DC) and the Pololu 5 V for the break-beam and opto LEDs. Never use C3 and USB-A together.

DIMMER KNOB: the LDP-2A knob must be reachable. Either seat the dimmer in a printed cradle under a 22 mm opening at the base's right rear corner or the underside lip (knob about 14-16 mm diameter, check on arrival), or use the CONSC-RF-12 remote dimmer and no opening. One knob dims every amber light, matching the viewer's single 'amber' 0..1 control.

UNDER-GLOW: replace SPEC base_glow (y 2-5, 3 mm) and the 6 x 4 mm undercut with a 5.3 x 5.3 mm groove for a QSG-0505 channel (5 x 5 mm, 1120 mm long) in an undercut at least 7 mm tall and 8 mm deep along the front bottom edge. Aim the opal face 30-45 degrees down and forward, at least 1.5 mm off the desk. The lit strip is 53 x 20.83 = 1104 mm. Feed it from the centre x = 0 through the existing cable chase (x -50..50) as two halves of about 552 mm, with a JST-SM at the feed and at any base-segment joint.

NECK LIGHT: a 5.3 x 5.3 mm groove, 150 mm long, at y 126-131 (5 mm tall, as in SPEC), but deepen it from 3 to 5.5 mm for a QSG-0505 piece cut from the 20 cm sample. The lit strip is 7 x 20.83 = 145.8 mm. Run a 2-wire 22 AWG lead down the neck beside the display cables.

INDICATORS (kb_charge_led, mouse_charge_led, dock_led): each is a single 20.83 mm segment of the same 3 mm 1800 K strip behind a 2 mm-tall window, lit through a printed clear or natural PETG light-guide (or a 2 mm acrylic sliver with a frosted face). Suggested window lengths are 21 mm (dock and keyboard; or 42 mm for two segments on the keyboard) and 16 mm (mouse, masking the 20.83 mm segment behind). A 30 mm window over one segment will show dim ends. Allow a 5 x 25 x 6 mm cavity behind each window for the segment and leads.

DOCK BREAK-BEAM: in the cradle slot walls, pockets of 20.6 x 10.6 x 9.6 mm for the emitter (left wall, x below 712) and receiver (right wall, x above 732), facing each other through 3.4 mm holes centred at y = 28.5 (4.5 mm above the slot floor at y 24) and z about +60 (away from the plug at z -60). Every printable slot insert needs coaxial 3.5 mm holes at the same y and z. Line the pockets and holes with IR-opaque material (black PETG or aluminium tape), because light or titanium-colour filament can pass IR. Route the 230 mm leads down into the cradle cavity (y 2.5-21). The light comes on only when the laptop is within about 3 mm of the floor, so the plug is engaged.

HALL ALTERNATIVE (only if the dock design gives the plug carriage at least 4 mm of travel under the laptop's weight): a US5881 (4.08 x 3.0 x 1.51) on the fixed carriage frame with the magnet on the sprung plug block, in slide-by geometry with a 2 mm gap.

THERMALS: internal heat is about 3 W from the GaN charger at 30 W out, up to about 8 W from the dock brick at 100 W (if it sits in the base), and up to 10.5 W from the LED strips at full (mostly shed through the aluminium channels). Print the power bay, brick bay and LED channel seats in PETG or ASA, not PLA (PLA softens around 55-60 C). Give the bay at least about 1500 mm2 of intake slots underneath (raised feet) and about 1500 mm2 of exhaust at the rear, and keep 5 mm or more of air around bricks. Default the dimmer to about 50 %.

POWER BUDGET (120 V wall), placeholders until the monitor and dock are chosen. Monitors 2 x 30 W typical / 2 x 60 W max. Dock brick: about 45 W typical, 140 W rating, so about 152 W at the wall at 92 %. GaN LV loads: LEDs 1.31 m x 8 W/m = 10.5 W max (0.875 A at 12 V), Qi transmitters up to about 3 x 10 W, logic 0.3 W, about 41 W DC or about 46 W at the wall. Total about 318 W max (2.65 A, 18 % of the 15 A / 1800 W strip) and about 120 W typical. Standby with lights off and the laptop out is about 2-3 W; the strip switch takes it to 0. LV rails: 12 V lighting 0.9 A max on C1 (3 A available); 12 V aux up to 3 A on C2; 5 V logic 40 mA.
PD DEPENDENCY: both triggers request a fixed 12 V PDO. Any replacement charger must list 12 V on its USB-C ports (Anker Prime does not), or the LEDs silently get 5 V. Note this in the build guide.

MONITOR POWER (coordinate with the display category): strongly prefer 27 in QHD monitors that use an external DC brick. The brick then lives in the base power bay on the strip, only low-voltage DC goes up the neck, and no mains sits inside the printed display shroud. If the monitors have internal PSUs, their stripped power boards must keep their original metal shield and insulating sheets inside the shroud, and two mains cords (C13 head about 38 x 24 x 15 mm) must pass the neck chase. Enlarge the chase to at least 30 x 45 mm, or route the cords before the heads go on.

DOCK BRICK BAY (coordinate with the dock category): reserve about 160 x 80 x 35 mm in the right wing / right end near x 450-640 with venting, its right-angle cord to the strip, and its DC or USB-C lead to the dock board under the cradle.
risks: The Tripp Lite datasheets give inconsistent heights (PS2404RA06B: 1.25 in vs 3.8 cm) and do not say which long face carries the outlets. Measure before freezing the power-bay geometry. US stock of the PS24xxRA strips is patchy (several resellers out of stock in Nov 2026).

Multi-port GaN chargers re-allocate power and briefly drop all ports when anything is plugged in or out. Using the spare C3 or USB-A for ad-hoc phone charging will blink the lights and reset the Qi transmitters. Also, C3 and USB-A together fall back to 5 V / 15 W on the Monoprice 46820.

Fixed-12 V PD triggers fall back to 5 V on chargers without a 12 V PDO (for example the Anker Prime A2683 USB-C ports), so the strips stay dark. Swapping chargers later can silently break the lighting.

The SuperLightingLED 1800 K strips and channels are not UL listed, ship from China (1-3 weeks; shipping charged under $299) and have unpublished strip thickness. COB colour and brightness vary between reels, so buy every amber light from one reel.
3 mm COB strips have tiny pads; clip-on connectors are unreliable. Solder leads and add strain relief, especially at the base-segment joints.

IR break-beam: IR-translucent filaments (light grey, titanium-colour, natural) can leak IR around the laptop and keep the light off, so the pockets need IR-opaque lining. Debris in the slot can falsely light it. The receiver output is only rated to the 5.5 V supply, so it must drive the 12 V segment through the opto.

The hall alternative depends on the dock carriage actually moving at least 4 mm under the laptop's weight, and can give a false 'seated' when the laptop rests on the plug tip. Its magnet sits near the laptop's lid sensor (harmless in clamshell mode, but note it).

The charge indicators rely on the Qi transmitter boards (another category) exposing a status-LED net. LED drive current, polarity and blink patterns are unknown, and dim if the board's LED current is under about 1 mA even with a high-CTR opto.
Thermal: PLA near the bricks or LED channels can creep. An enclosed surge strip (MOVs) is avoided on purpose; do not substitute a surge strip inside the base.

Mains safety boundary: the plan keeps all mains inside certified products (UL 1363 strip, UL/ETL cords, ETL charger, the bricks). Stripped monitors with internal PSU boards would put mains circuitry inside a user-made printed shroud, which breaks that boundary unless the monitors use external bricks or the original shields and insulation are retained.
The Vishay 4N33 opto is obsolete; use TLP627M (current) and verify CTR and IC against the Toshiba datasheet (did=16914) before ordering.
open_questions: Monitor choice: does each 27 in QHD monitor use an external DC brick or an internal PSU, which IEC inlet (C14, C6 or C8), and what are its typical and max watts? This decides the cords, neck-chase size and power budget.

verify.summary:
I checked all 25 primary and alternate parts in the power-lighting report against primary sources: Tripp Lite, Toshiba, Lite-On, Hynetek, Melexis and WAGO data sheets, the Monoprice tech drawing, the JST catalog, and live vendor pages fetched 2026-11-07. 9 are verified, 15 are corrected and 1 is rejected. The main dimensions are right: power strip 31.8 x 609.6 x 40.9 mm with outlets 144 mm apart; Monoprice 46820 charger 98.81 x 76.31 x 23.10 mm; Pololu regulator 13 x 10 x 3 mm; Adafruit 5807 24.5 x 20.2 x 4.9 mm; LED channel 5 x 5 mm with a 3 mm inner width; strip cut pitch 20.83 mm.

Findings that change the build:

1. **Charger port plan.** The Monoprice label says that with USB-C1 and USB-C2 both in use, the split is 65 W + 35 W. That caps C2 at about 2.9 A at 12 V, not the 3 A the report budgets. The HUSB238 chip on the Adafruit 5807 only accepts a power level whose current meets its request. Set to 12 V and 3 A on that 35 W port, it skips 12 V and gives 9 V instead. Fix: put the Qi/aux bus on C1, put the 0.9 A lighting on C2, and set the 5807 to 2 A. The 5807's current jumpers are actually 1 A (the default), 2 A, or 3 A with both jumpers open, so it starts at 5 V and 1 A.

2. **Out-of-stock parts.**
   - The LDP-2A dimmer is out of stock, backorder only, expected 12/23/26. Use the same-size SuperLightingLED CONSC-DIM-03 ($6.99, in stock, 61 x 33 x 32 mm, 2 A, same vendor as the strip).
   - Adafruit 368 is out of stock at Adafruit; buy it from DigiKey.
   - The TLP627M order code should be TLP627M(E, not "TLP627M(F". It has 0 stock at LCSC and a 24-week lead at DigiKey.

3. **4N33 rejected.** It is obsolete at Vishay, onsemi, Everlight and TT, and I found no Lite-On version. Use the Lite-On LTV-815 instead (4-pin, CTR at least 600 % at 1 mA, 35 V, 80 mA, LCSC $0.25). It also covers the TLP627M stock problem.

4. **LED channel.** The vendor charges extra long-shipping fees for 2 m lengths on orders under 10 pieces. Buy 2 x 1 m ($9.96) and cut two 560 mm under-glow halves that meet at the centre feed point, plus the 150 mm neck piece from the offcuts. No separate sample is needed.

5. **Break-beam geometry.** Adafruit's drawing shows the LED on the 20 x 10 mm face, centred across the 10 mm width and about 5 mm from one end, with a 2.4 mm mounting hole 10 mm away. The beam hole must be offset from the pocket centre. The beam (about 5 mm up) sits only about 1.5 mm below a laptop resting on the plug tip (6.5 mm), so check it on the bench.

6. **WAGO dimensions.** Current WAGO sheets give 221-412 as 13.2 x 8.4 x 18.8 mm and 221-413 as 18.8 x 8.4 x 18.6 mm. The file cited for 221-412 is actually the 221-415 sheet.

7. **Power strip mounting and safety.** The strip's clips take #8 or #10 screws, so use M4 heat-set inserts, not M3. A UL 1363 strip fixed into furniture formally falls under UL 962A; keep it clip-mounted and removable.

8. **Smaller fixes.**
   - The alternate Super Bright LEDs strip's buy link selects the 4000 K variant; the 2200 K link is given above.
   - The US5881 Hall sensor is in production, not a legacy part.

   - The PS2404RA06B appears to have better stock than the primary: CompSource $32.02 with 522 in stock, per a search snippet.

design_implications: BUDGET: primary set at list = K3 Ultra 109.99 + Magic Tag 29.99 + Cobra HyperSpeed 99.99 + puck 29.99 + 2x Anker 313 23.99 = $317.94 (~$68 over the $250 target; ~$285 at typical street prices). On-budget combos: K3 Ultra + Magic Tag + Lenovo Go + 2 pads = $247.95, or ZAGG Pro Keyboard 12 + Cobra HyperSpeed + puck + 2 pads = $247.95, or ZAGG + Lenovo Go + 2 pads = $177.96. The desk mat is extra ($77-85).

KEYBOARD POCKET: keep the 376 x 136 universal pocket but add printed per-keyboard locator inserts, the same idea as the laptop cradle inserts. K3 Ultra insert opening 322.6 x 128 (1 mm clearance each side), plus a ~12 x 30 mm relief at the left-rear for the USB-C sled plug and fold. Locating the keyboard to +/-1-2 mm is what makes a single-coil Qi transmitter work.

KEYBOARD HEIGHT: the real board is ~2x the placeholder. K3 Ultra measures 20.0 mm front and 25.5 mm rear including keycaps and feet (placeholder: 9 -> 13 mm). Resting at y=16-18, the keycaps reach y~41.5-43.5, 5.5-7.5 mm above the 36 mm rim. Options: raise the base/rim to ~44-46 mm (within the 36-50 mm brief) or accept a proud keyboard. Do not lower the pocket floor: the transmitter needs about 12.5 mm under it.

ONE keyboard transmitter, not two: replace qi_coils_kb_x [-170,-10] with one adjustable coil. With the K3 Ultra + Magic Tag folded around the LEFT edge, the receiver centre lands roughly 40 mm in from the keyboard's left edge and 25-30 mm forward of its rear edge (estimate). Mount the transmitter in a printed carrier on a slotted rail (+/-20 mm in x, +/-15 mm in z) and lock it with screws after a charge test. For the ZAGG alternate, put the coil under the keyboard centre.

MOUSE POCKET: the 82 x 134 pocket lets the mouse wander +/-10 mm, which is too loose for the 33 mm Razer puck. Add a printed insert sized 66 x 123.5 for the Cobra (119.6 x 62.5 x 38.1). Put the transmitter coil centre on the mouse centreline under the puck, est. ~35 mm forward of the mouse's rear edge (rear-centre, as on Razer's Basilisk photo). Verify on the real mouse; the carrier needs +/-10 mm adjustment. Lenovo Go insert: 64 x 102.

Z-STACK UNDER EACH POCKET (Anker 313 embedded intact): base bottom skin y=0-2 (or a removable hatch); pad 100 x 100 x 11.2 at y~2.8-14.0 in a printed cradle, coil centred; solid printed pocket floor 1.0 mm over the coil at y=14-15 (100% infill, PETG/ASA); non-metallic skin <=1 mm at y=15-16; device rests at y=16 instead of y=18. That keeps plastic between pad top and device at <=2 mm, inside Anker's 'through cases up to 5 mm'. Replace the 2 mm tray_pad with a 1 mm skin (thin felt, PU or printed TPU) at least over a 60 mm circle.

METAL/MAGNET KEEP-OUT: no metal spine, steel inserts, screws, foil, magnets or LED PCBs over or within ~10 mm of each 100 x 100 pad footprint, and keep steel >=5 mm below the pad's ferrite. Route the spine behind or around the pocket coil zones, and make the pocket floors fully plastic (the old 'Ti floor with 54 mm windows' no longer applies).

SERVICE AND POWER: each pad needs its own >=5 V/2 A USB port from the certified charger in the base (QC/9 V not needed: the receivers are 5 W BPP). Run two 0.3-0.5 m USB-A/C to micro-B cables, right-angle micro plugs saving ~10 mm, through cable channels with strain relief. Give each pad a screwed bottom hatch with a >=104 x 104 mm opening so pads can be swapped. Laptop USB ports are not enough (Anker warns against 5 V/1 A sources).

HEAT: each transmitter dissipates ~2-4 W while charging, inside a closed printed base. Print pad cradles and pocket floors in PETG or ASA (not PLA), add vent slots from the cradle to the underside or rear channel, and leave the Anker temperature protection in place (do not shim the pad).

CHARGE LEDs (kb_charge_led, mouse_charge_led): the Anker pad's own LED is blue and hidden. Drive the amber indicators from an inline per-pad USB current sense (idle vs charging current) or a light sensor on the pad LED; hand this to the power-lighting design.

KEYBOARD SLED INSTALL: plug the Magic Tag into the K3 Ultra's left-side USB-C (USB-C, Win/Mac and BT/2.4G switches are all on the left face toward the rear). Fold the ribbon 180 deg around the left edge and tape the <=1 mm pad flat to the underside, clear of the flip-out rear feet. It stays in the 2 mm foot gap, so the board still sits on its feet. Leave the BT/2.4G switch reachable beside the plug.

CAD SOURCES: import Keychron's official K3_Ultra_8K_US_Full-Model-20260716.stp and _Bottom_Case-20260716.stp (github.com/Keychron/Keychron-Keyboards-Hardware-Design, files on keychron.co:34568, which timed out from this container) as reference bodies for the insert, port position and foot locations. No manufacturer CAD was found for Razer or Lenovo mice: model the mouse as an envelope box.

DESK MAT in CAD: deskmat [820,3,300] -> Oakywood 900 x 3.0 x 300 (or custom 820 x 300 x 3), or Orbitkey Pro Slim 800 x 4.9 x 310. Update the work-pose drop heights by the mat thickness (3.0 vs 4.9 mm).

AMBER LIGHTING: K3 Ultra per-key RGB can be set to static amber (Keychron Launcher), and the Cobra HyperSpeed underglow + logo to amber (Razer Synapse). Neither needs CAD parts; the spec's mouse_glow at the mouse rear lines up with the Cobra's underglow.
risks: The Razer Wireless Charging Puck (RC21-01990200-R3U1) was OUT OF STOCK on razer.com on 2026-11-07; only Micro Center showed stock. Razer only promises charging on its own chargers and 'other inductive chargers with proper coil alignment'.

Qi alignment: a single A11-type coil (OD 44, ID 20.5 mm) with a small 33 mm receiver has only a few mm of lateral tolerance (no normative figure found). Without tight locator inserts and an adjustable carrier, charging will be intermittent.
Distance: Anker 313 is rated through <=5 mm of case. The original stack (2 mm floor + 2 mm pad + the pad's own cover + the device's shell) can exceed that, so keep the 1 mm floor + <=1 mm skin.

False FOD trips: the K3 Ultra's aluminium plate/frame and the Cobra's internals sit above the receivers. If the Anker pad flashes 'metal obstruction', add a 0.3 mm flexible ferrite sheet between the Magic Tag and the keyboard bottom.

The USB-C sled plug sticks out ~8-10 mm on the left side and could be knocked or levered when lifting the keyboard out, stressing the keyboard's port. Use the Short variant and consider a printed clip guard.
Internal receiver mod (alternate) means opening a Li-po keyboard and soldering to VBUS: puncture or short risk, and it voids the warranty. Do this only with the battery disconnected.
Heat in a closed printed base can soften PLA; Qi efficiency is ~70%, so 1.5-2.5 W is lost per active pad.
The Anker 313 uses legacy micro-USB, and its revisions or sale may change. Re-check dims (100 x 100 x 11.2) on arrival before printing cradles.
Budget: the primary set is ~$318 at list against a $250 target.
The ZAGG alternate has a membrane, no backlight and Bluetooth only, and its dimensions come from reviews, not a spec sheet.
The Lenovo Go alternate is compact (100 mm) and its dims vary between sources (100x62x34 vs 101x59x34).
Oakywood ships from Poland: US import duties or brokerage can add cost and delay. Custom sizes take 3-5 weeks.
Generic or non-certified Qi modules (Adafruit 2162, QST, marketplace PCBAs) may lack effective FOD, so a dropped coin or key in a pocket can heat up. Prefer the certified pad.

verify.summary:
I checked all 11 primary and alternate parts against primary sources on 2026-11-07. Results: 7 verified, 2 corrected, 2 rejected.

**Rejected**
- **Lenovo Go mouse (4Y51C21217) is discontinued.** The report's CDW link now says 'We no longer carry' it and shows the replacement, the Lenovo Multi-Device Wireless Mouse X9 Edition 4Y51R29290. Lenovo's datasheet for the X9 gives 59 x 101 x 34 mm, 75 g, native Qi. CDW price is $51.99 advertised ($58.99 list), in stock.
- **Adafruit 1901 internal receiver mod.** It is out of stock. The mod also means opening a Li-po keyboard and joining a second 5 V source onto VBUS without a diode, so a plugged-in USB-C cable would feed back into the receiver. Use the NILLKIN Magic Tag Type-C Long (6902048128903) instead.

**Corrected**
- **NILLKIN Magic Tag Type-C Short.** The 82 x 48 mm figure is the pad only. Nillkin's graphic gives 100 mm overall (Long: 111 mm). The coil sits about 50 mm from the pad's tail-side edge. Folded around the K3 Ultra's left edge, the coil lands about 45-55 mm in from that edge, not 40.
  - The pad hangs off a rear-left port about 23 mm from the rear edge, so it overlaps the left-rear foot (about 15 mm from the rear edge, under the port cluster). It cannot lie flat as described. It needs a 45-degree fold in the ribbon (coil then about 45-50 mm from the rear edge) or the Long variant.
  - The transmitter carrier must cover x 35-60 mm from the keyboard's left edge and z 15-55 mm from its rear edge. In params.py, the 100 x 100 Anker pad would run up to about 22 mm past the pocket's rear wall (pocket rear wall z=-6, pad edge down to z~-28).
- **Anker 313 (A2503).** The 100 x 100 x 11.2 mm size is confirmed by Anker's manual (V08), as are the 5V 2A / 9V 2A input and the $23.99 in-stock price. Corrections:
  - Weight is 63 g, not 67.
  - The LED also flashes green for overvoltage.
  - The manual sets a 40 C maximum ambient during use and recommends below 25 C for full-speed charging. This is a hard number for venting the closed printed base.

**Verified**
- **Keychron K3 Ultra 8K.** All six ANSI SKUs are $109.99 and available. Dimensions from Keychron's spec table and side graphic:
  - 320.62 x 126 mm
  - 16.55 / 20.1 mm without keycaps; 20.0 / 25.5 mm with keycaps
  - 2 mm feet, ABS bottom case
  - Ports on the left side face, toward the rear

  The STEP files are confirmed in Keychron's repo README, but their download host times out, so the port position is still an estimate (about 23 mm from the rear edge, about 6.5 mm up). Two notes:
  - Its 2.4 GHz receiver is USB Type-A, as is the Cobra's dongle. The dock needs USB-A ports, or the user switches to Bluetooth.
  - The flip-out feet must stay folded in the pocket, or the receiver lifts off the coil.
- **ZAGG Pro Keyboard 12 (103210887).** $69.99, Qi confirmed. Its dimensions come from a review only (about 295 x 130 x 19 mm).
- **Razer Cobra HyperSpeed (RZ01-05570100-R3U1).** $99.99, in stock. 119.6 x 62.5 x 38.1 mm, 62 g, and Razer lists the puck as a compatible accessory.
- **Razer Wireless Charging Puck (RC21-01990200-R3U1).** $29.99, still out of stock. Razer gives about 33 x 4.6 mm and says it works on 'other inductive chargers with proper coil alignment'. Supply risk: Razer now ships a 'Puck V2' with the Mouse Dock V2 Pro, and its behaviour on third-party Qi pads is not documented.
- **Adafruit 2162.** $26.95, in stock. Specs match: 53 x 53 x 4 mm coil plate, 55 x 37 x 6 mm board, 2-8 mm charging distance. It has no certification or foreign-object detection, so keep it as the alternate only.
- **Oakywood Felt & Cork mat (1501FEAL).** $77, 900 x 300 x 3 mm, cork base 0.8 mm, 5-year warranty. US duties and taxes are calculated at checkout.
- **Orbitkey Desk Mat Pro Slim (WDS1-BLK-105).** $85, 800 x 310 x 4.9 mm on Orbitkey's page.

**Budget**
- The primary set at list totals $317.94; the report's arithmetic is correct.
- With the X9 Edition: K3 Ultra + Magic Tag + X9 + 2x Anker 313 = $239.95.

**Still open**
- K3 Ultra port and foot positions (need the official STEP).
- The Cobra's puck-bay centre (measure on arrival).
- Magic Tag thickness (unpublished).

design_implications: PRINT ENVELOPE IS THE MAIN CONSTRAINT: a Bambu 256 x 256 x 256 bed means every tile must fit about 245 x 245 mm (keep 5 mm margin). The base is 300 mm deep, so it cannot be one tile front-to-back; a 300 mm part only fits diagonally if it is 62 mm wide or less. Split the base into 2 rows x 6 columns: a rear 'spine' row about 140 deep and a front 'pocket' row about 160 deep. Make the joint lines deliberate reveals. The neck (320 mm wide at the bottom) and the cradle (260 mm deep) also exceed 256, so split them or shrink them to 245 or less. Each 612 x 363 monitor back needs about 3 x 2 tiles, so about 12-16 shroud tiles in total.

LOAD PATH: monitors -> 3/16 in steel wing bracket (2 x 10 deg bends) -> 2x 2040 posts (80 x 40 column) -> 1/4 in steel spine plate (600 x 130, z -144..-14, x -300..300) -> 3M SJ5023 feet on the desk. No printed part carries monitor load. The shroud hangs off the bracket with M4 screws into M4x8.1 inserts, with 1.5-3 mm clearance plus 1.6 mm foam to the monitor backs.

DEPTH BUDGET BEHIND THE SEAM: with the seam axis at z=-62, a wing plane at w=-50 (VESA boss + spacer) and bend lines at x=+/-40, the bracket's centre panel lands at z of about -105.7. The posts behind it need 20 mm (weak axis) or 40 mm (strong axis), pushing them to z of about -131 or -151. The base rear edge is z=-150, so either move the seam axis forward about 10-20 mm, make the base about 310-320 deep, or turn the 2040s weak-axis fore-aft. Real 27 in monitors are 40-60 mm deep at the VESA boss, against the 12 mm stripped modules in params.display, so the shroud depth (45) and keel must grow to about 80-100 mm behind the glass.

VERTICAL STACK IN THE BASE: the cavity is y 2.5..27.5 (25 mm). A 1/4 in plate (6.35, +0.38 tol) plus a 20 mm rail on top is 26.7 mm and does not fit with a printed floor. Either let the steel plate replace the printed floor in the rear zone (plate y 0..6.35, rails beside it, not on top), or raise the base height to about 42 mm (the brief allows 36-50).

FRONT STRIP: params leave only 14 mm (z 132..146) between the pocket walls and the front wall, which is too narrow for a 2020. Use a 1/4 x 3/4 in steel bar on edge (19 tall x 6.35, 1100 long, 1.04 kg), or move both pocket centres from z 62 to 54 and use a second 2020 x 1200.

QI CLEARANCE: no steel under the pockets or within about 20 mm of the coil footprints (coils about 50 mm diameter at x=-170, -10, 250, z=62). Ballast goes in the rear zone, the front strip, and the left wing (x -630..-300, which is free now that there is no computer in the base). Keep magnets at least 30 mm from the coils.

TIP-OVER (scripts/tipover.py): thanks to the 10 deg toe-in, each monitor's CoM sits at about z=-29, y=338, about 109 mm in front of rear feet at z=-138. Without ballast the system tips back only at 20-26 deg (the IEC 62368-1 10 deg tilt test passes) and needs about 43-56 N pushed back at the screen top (y 520), against an IEC horizontal-force guide of 13% of weight, about 30 N. Recommended: the 3.9 kg spine plate plus the 1.04 kg front bar (about 5 kg of steel) gives 53-59 N rear push and 90-105 N forward pull, even with the monitor CoM 25 mm further back. Optional wing plates (2x 1/4 in, about 6 kg) raise rear push to about 71-77 N. The rear feet MUST be at the very back edge (z <= -138; params feet at -122 cut the margin about 20%), and the segments must be rigidly tied to the plate and rails, otherwise the effective footprint shrinks.

TOE-IN TRIM: the SendCutSend bend tolerance is +/-2 deg on parts over 24 in. Plan 4.6 x 10 mm vertical VESA slots (seam height alignment) and allow M4 washer shims (1 mm over the 100 mm pattern = 0.57 deg) to equalise the toe-in. The seam gap is set by sliding the monitors along the slots before the shroud goes on.

INSERT BOSSES (manufacturer tables): M3x5.7: hole 4.0, depth >= 6.7, boss OD >= 7.8 (wall 1.6). M4x8.1: hole 5.6 (ruthex) / 5.7 (CNC Kitchen), depth >= 9.1, boss OD >= 10.5. M5x9.5: hole 6.4/6.5, depth >= 10.5, boss OD >= 12.3. Model to the purchased brand, or use 5.65/6.45 as a compromise.
MAGNET POCKETS: 6.55 dia x 3.4 for K&J D42 (6.35 x 3.17), or 6.2 x 3.2 for supermagnete S-06-03-N (6 x 3). Glue them in with CA or epoxy; mind the polarity.
EXTRUSION HOLES DIFFER BY SOURCE: ZYLtech 2020 centre hole is 5.0 mm (M6), ZYLtech 2040 is 5.2 (M6), Misumi HFS5 is 4.2 (M5). Slot width is 6 mm on all. The CAD should put the source in a parameter.

HEAT / MATERIAL MAP: base shell, cradle, display shroud and diffusers in PETG/PETG-CF/ASA (HDT 68-100 C). PLA only for cool trim such as the badge, oxblood inlays and covers away from the USB-C plug (PLA HDT 52-62 C). Keep shroud vent area so the monitors' own vents are not choked (monitors run about 20-35 W each).
PAINT ALLOWANCE: primer plus metallic plus clear adds about 0.1-0.2 mm per side. Leave 0.3 mm per side on inlays (deck liner, oxblood panels, seam strip) and on slot inserts for the laptop.

FILAMENT MASS (scripts/filament.py, solid-equivalent area x wall): base about 3.8 kg (3.0 if the steel plate replaces the floor in the rear zone), shroud about 2.4 kg (12-16 tiles, 2.0 mm skins, 90 mm deep), neck about 0.35 kg, cradle plus inserts about 0.8 kg, diffusers about 0.05 kg. Net about 7.3 kg; buy about 9-10 kg (titanium PETG 5 kg, graphite PETG-CF 3 kg, oxblood 1, diffuser 1). Filament cost about $230-250. Print time about 75-120 h.
MASS AND HANDLING: the complete station is about 29-35 kg with monitors, so it is a two-person lift. Consider recessed hand-holds under the wing ends and do not lift by the shroud.
risks: The custom wing bracket and post have no third-party load rating. Calculated stresses are below 5 MPa against 283 MPa yield, but use 8.8+ bolts, threadlocker and a 2x-load hang test (24 kg) before mounting the monitors. The VIVO MOUNT-VW02A (10 kg/arm rated) is the fallback.

SendCutSend part prices are estimates only; instant quotes need a file upload. Budget about $140 for the plate, bracket and front bar, plus about $40 for powder coat. OSH Cut is the alternative vendor.
Bambu stock on 2026-11-07: PETG HF Gray 33101 and Dark Gray 33103, PLA Sparkle Crimson Red 13200, ASA Black and PC Transparent are out of stock. Swap per the alternates or wait for a restock.
PETG-CF and PLA-CF need a hardened-steel nozzle. ASA needs an enclosed printer (not the open-frame A1).
Tile seams and warping on many 245 mm PETG/ASA tiles: use alignment pins, magnets or inserts, glue, a brim, and print flat-face-down to keep visible faces clean.

The rear-tip margin depends on the rear feet being at the very back edge and on the whole base acting as one rigid body. Loose segment joints or inset feet reduce it (with feet at z=-122, push resistance drops about 20%).
Real monitors' VESA depth, back profile and weight are unknown until the monitor is chosen. The bracket, post position and shroud depth all depend on them.
Bare A36 steel rusts. Coat the plates; SendCutSend powder coat max is 31 x 37 in, plating max 23 x 23 in.
Metallic spray finishes scuff on the base rim and pocket edges where hands rest; a satin clear (or 2K clear with a respirator) is needed.
Ballast or the front bar near the Qi coils could cause heating or foreign-object-detection trips. Keep at least 20 mm of steel clearance from the coil footprints.
Extrusion section properties come from the Misumi equivalent profile; ZYLtech publishes no drawing (only centre-hole sizes).
open_questions: Which exact 27 in QHD monitors? Need width, height, depth at the VESA boss, VESA centre height above the bottom edge, mass, and the back profile near the inner bezel. These set the bracket wing length (VESA centre at u of about 314 mm), the post length (about 300-340 mm) and the shroud depth.
Which Bambu printer (A1 open-frame vs P1S/X1C/P2S/H2 enclosed), and is a hardened-steel nozzle available? This decides ASA vs PETG and whether CF filaments can be used.
Fixed geometry (custom wing bracket, primary) or adjustable tilt/swivel (VIVO MOUNT-VW02A, alternate)? Can the shroud tolerate the alternate's 127 mm profile?
Can the CAD move the seam axis forward about 10-20 mm or deepen the base to about 310-320 mm, so the bracket and posts fit inside z >= -150?
Base height: keep 36 mm (the steel plate must replace the printed floor in the rear zone) or raise it to about 42 mm (simpler rail and plate stacking)?
Raw filament colour, or primer plus titanium metallic paint on the titanium parts? This decides whether PETG HF Gray or cheap PETG Basic Gray is bought.
Pockets: move them 8 mm rearward so a second 2020 rail fits at the front, or keep the steel on-edge front bar?
Real titanium seam strip (6.35 mm minimum width at SendCutSend) or a printed mullion painted titanium (the 4 mm concept width)?

verify.summary:
I checked all 31 parts marked primary or alternate against my own downloads of primary sources. Results: 16 verified, 13 corrected, 2 unverifiable, 0 rejected. Nothing is unsafe, and every part exists except one wrong MPN (ABMM-A-C0, replaced below).

Things that change the CAD or the plan:
1. Wing bracket (SendCutSend HRP-188): all the vendor numbers match SendCutSend's own specs file (thickness 4.78 +/-0.15, inside radius 3.18, k-factor 0.32, bend deduction 8.2, minimum flange 15.7, bend tolerance +/-1 deg up to 24 in and +/-2 deg over, maximum part 1117x762). But the load check only covered the in-plane direction. A flat 4.78 x 120 wing is weak fore-aft: about 27 N/mm at the VESA centre, and a 20 N push moves a monitor's outer edge about 5.7 mm (first mode about 10 Hz). Expect wobble and seam misalignment. Fix: make each wing a separate bent channel with return flanges, bolted to a flat centre plate. Also, if the outer M5 slots sit at x=+/-30 with bend lines at +/-40, the holes are 10 mm from the bend; SendCutSend's minimum is 12.4 mm. Move the bends to about +/-45 or more. The bracket can be powder coated but not plated.
2. Neck posts: the report contradicts itself. Slots "10 and 30 mm from the edge" means the 40 mm faces point forward, which is the weak axis fore-aft (I = 2.7e4 mm4), not the claimed strong axis (1.03e5). Pick one in the CAD. Use M6x20 (not M6x16) into ZYLtech's 5.2 mm centre holes, or countersunk M6 so heads stay above the 7.6 mm SJ5023 feet.
3. The 1100 mm front bar is too long for SendCutSend powder coat (31x37 in max) or plating (23x23 in max). Paint it at home or split it in two.
4. VIVO MOUNT-VW02A: $34.99, in stock, 10 kg per arm, M6x30 arm screws, VESA-plate mounting with M5x12 + washers + nuts. VIVO describes it as a curved rail, not the "straight bar" in the report.
5. The whole Bambu PETG HF line (all 15 colours, including Gray 33101 and Dark Gray 33103) is out of stock on the US store. PETG Basic is fully in stock at $13.99 per refill, with better heat resistance (HDT 68/71 C). Its Gray 30107 is much darker (#7F7E83), so it only works if primed and painted; Dark Beige 30403 (#DBC8B6) is the raw-colour option.
6. Corrected part numbers and prices: Everbilt 801097 now returns 404; the same store SKU 368148 is model 0750 at $41.51 per bar. ZYLtech nut SKUs are HW-M5-HAMMER-100PK ($9.95) and HW-M5-SPRNG-T-NUT-100PK ($12.95). Panduit ABMM-A-C0 does not exist; use ABMM-AT-C0 (black). Rust-Oleum 245220 is an 11 oz can at $9.49 (Home Depot). MONTANA 087092 is $12.31. The cited RSP Supply 650045 is a 20x40 profile, not 20x20.
7. Verified without changes: ZYLtech 2020 1200 mm rail ($15.54, centre hole 5.0) and 2040 400 mm post ($10.14, centre hole 5.2); Misumi HFS5 section data; ruthex and CNC Kitchen insert tables (the report's boss diameters are on the conservative side, which is fine); K&J D42-N52 and supermagnete S-06-03-N; Bumpon SJ5023 (20.6 x 7.6) and SJ5018 (12.7 x 5.8); VHB 5952 at 1.1 mm; Bambu ASA, PETG-CF, PLA-CF, PLA Basic and PETG Translucent prices, stock, data sheets and colour codes.

Unverifiable: Rust-Oleum 260510 (no reachable primary page; verified substitute is Rust-Oleum Automotive 249279) and the screw kit, which has no SKU. Prices I could not check: SendCutSend parts (need a file quote), Misumi (blocks bots), Bumpon packs, and the ruthex Amazon US listings. The web-search budget ran out partway through; after that I only fetched manufacturer and retailer pages directly.
